name: LM331N_NOPB
title: LM231, LM331 (and A grades): precision voltage-to-frequency converters in 8-pin PDIP
summary: A monolithic voltage-to-frequency converter that also works backwards as a frequency-to-voltage converter. A band-gap reference sets a precision current, a one-shot timer set by an external R and C gates that current out of pin 1, and an input comparator starts each timing cycle, so the pulse rate on the open-collector output tracks the input voltage. Full-scale frequency can be set anywhere from 1 Hz to 100 kHz, linearity is 0.01 % maximum, and the part runs from a single 4 V to 40 V supply or from split rails. LM231 parts are rated for -25 °C to 85 °C and LM331 parts for 0 °C to 70 °C; the A grades hold gain drift to ±50 ppm/°C maximum. LM331N/NOPB is the standard-grade LM331 in PDIP.

pins.name: IOUT
pins.function: Switched current source output. During each timing period the precision current i (1.90 V / RS) flows out of this pin; otherwise it is steered to ground.

pins.name: IREF
pins.function: Reference current pin, held at about 1.9 V by the band-gap. The resistor RS from this pin to ground sets the current i.

pins.name: FOUT
pins.function: Frequency output, an open-collector transistor that is on during each timing period. Needs a pull-up resistor.

pins.name: RC
pins.function: Timing node for the one-shot: Rt to the supply and Ct to ground. The timer ends its period when this pin reaches 2/3 of VS, and the reset transistor then discharges it.

pins.name: THRESH
pins.function: Threshold input, the inverting side of the input comparator.

pins.name: COMPIN
pins.function: Comparator input, the non-inverting side: a cycle starts when this pin is above pin 6.

circuits.title: Simple stand-alone V-to-F converter, ±0.03 % typical linearity (f = 10 Hz to 11 kHz)
circuits.description: A positive input of 0 V to 10 V gives 0 Hz to 10 kHz with no op amp. The pin-6 integrating node (RL in parallel with CL) is fed by the pin-1 current pulses and leaks back through RL; the comparator fires whenever pin 7 rises above it. RIN matches RL so the comparator bias currents cancel, CIN filters the input, the 47 ohm resistor under CL adds hysteresis, RS (12 k plus a 5 k rheostat) trims gain, and the optional 22 k from a pot across the supplies trims offset. Pin 3 is open collector, pulled up to the logic rail.

parts.note: optional offset adjust, ends to +VS and -VS
gain adjust rheostat; stable, low temperature coefficient

circuits.title: Standard test circuit: precision V-to-F converter
circuits.description: The circuit the electrical characteristics are measured in. An op amp integrator (A1 with CF) replaces the RC network: the input current through RIN from a negative input is balanced by the charge pulses from pin 1, which sits at the op amp's virtual ground. The integrator output drives pin 7 through 2.2 k; pin 6 sits at the threshold set by the 10 k / 10 k divider from VS. A 1N4002 runs from ground to the integrator output. A1's non-inverting input takes an optional offset trim from a pot across the supplies. 0 V to -10 V gives 0 Hz to 10 kHz.

parts.note: op amp with low input offset (voltage and current); pins 2 inverting input, 3 non-inverting input, 6 output, 7 positive supply, 4 negative supply
10 kΩ is needed with VS from 4.5 V to 8 V; with VS from 8 V to 22 V either 5 kΩ or 10 kΩ

circuits.title: Precision V-to-F converter, 100 kHz full scale, ±0.03 % non-linearity
circuits.description: The precision converter reworked for 100 kHz: CT drops to 330 pF and CF to 470 pF, 0.001 µF bypasses the lower threshold resistor and A1's non-inverting input, and RS becomes 5 k plus a 2 k gain rheostat. A 2N2222 with two 20 k resistors hangs on the pin-2 reference node. 0 V to -10 V gives 0 Hz to 100 kHz.

parts.note: op amp with low input offset (voltage and current); pins 2 inverting input, 3 non-inverting input, 6 output, 7 positive supply, 4 negative supply

circuits.title: Simple frequency-to-voltage converter, 10 kHz full scale, ±0.06 % non-linearity
circuits.description: A pulse train at fIN is coupled through 470 pF into pin 6, which rests at VS through 10 k; pin 7 sits at a fixed fraction of VS set by 10 k and 68 k. Each falling edge fires the one-shot, and the pin-1 current pulses average into RL with 1 µF across it, giving a DC output proportional to frequency. Pin 3 is grounded and unused.

circuits.title: Precision frequency-to-voltage converter, 10 kHz full scale with 2-pole filter, ±0.01 % non-linearity maximum
circuits.description: The same input network as the simple F-to-V converter, with Rx in place of the fixed lower resistor at pin 7. The pin-1 current is smoothed by C3 and then by an op amp stage (100 k, RF, C4) that inverts, buffers and forms a second filter pole, so VOUT is negative for positive frequency. Supply 4.5 V to 20 V.

circuits.title: Light intensity to frequency converter
circuits.description: A phototransistor feeds current through 10 k into the joined pins 1 and 6, with 0.001 µF from that node to ground; pins 7 and 2 are tied together at the reference node with 5 k plus a 5 k rheostat to ground. The output on pin 3, pulled up by 3.3 k, has a frequency proportional to light, 100 kHz full scale. Supply 5 V to 15 V.

circuits.title: Temperature to frequency converter
circuits.description: An LM234/LM334 current source set by 2.32 k gives 0.1 µA/K into the joined pins 1 and 6, smoothed by 0.1 µF; pins 7 and 2 are tied together at the reference node with 12 k plus a 5 k rheostat to ground. The output on pin 3, pulled up by 22 k, runs at 10 Hz/K. Supply 4.5 V to 20 V.

circuits.title: Remote V-to-F converter with 2-wire transmitter and receiver
circuits.description: A remote converter is powered and read over one twisted pair. At the far end an LM340LAZ-5.0 makes +5 V for the converter from the line, with 0.1 µF across the line; the converter's open-collector output has 750 ohm to the +5 V rail. At the supply end the line is fed from +15 V through 75 ohm, and the frequency output is taken from the line side of that resistor.

circuits.title: V-to-F converter with square-wave output using a divide-by-2 flip-flop

operation.text: A temperature-compensated band-gap gives about 1.9 VDC, held steady for VS from 3.9 V to 40 V and typically moving less than ½ % over a 100 °C span. A current pump holds pin 2 at 1.9 V, so the resistor RS from pin 2 to ground draws i = 1.90 V / RS. A precision current mirror copies i to a current switch, which sends it either out of pin 1 or to ground according to the state of an R-S flip-flop. Accuracy over temperature is kept with supplies as low as 4 V.

The input comparator watches pins 7 and 6. When pin 7 rises above pin 6 it sets the flip-flop; the set state enables both the pin-3 output transistor and the current switch. The external Rt charges Ct on pin 5; when pin 5 reaches 2/3 of VCC the timer comparator resets the flip-flop, turning the current switch off and the reset transistor on to discharge Ct. The period is 1.1 × Rt × Ct.

Should pin 7 remain higher than pin 6 at the moment pin 5 reaches 2/3 VCC, no reset occurs and current keeps flowing out of pin 1 to drive pin 6 above pin 7. This happens at start-up and when the input is overloaded; while it lasts the output frequency is 0. Normal pulses return as soon as the input comes back into range.
Pin 2 is regulated at 1.90 VDC for any i between 10 µA and 500 µA. It can serve as a voltage reference for other parts, provided no current is drawn from it that would upset the converter's accuracy.

The output transistor pulls pin 3 down with roughly 50 Ω of on-resistance. Under overvoltage the output current is limited to less than 50 mA. The open-collector output can drive 3 TTL loads or be pulled up to as much as 40 V, and survives a short to VCC; its pulses can be passed through a simple photo isolator to cross high common-mode voltages.

In the simplest converter the input V1 goes to pin 7 and an RC network (RL in parallel with CL) sits on pin 6 and pin 1. When V1 exceeds the pin 6 voltage Vx the comparator starts the timer; for 1.1 RtCt the current i flows into CL and carries Vx above V1. When the period ends CL discharges through RL until Vx falls back to V1, and the next cycle begins. The current into CL averages i × 1.1 RtCt × f, the current out is Vx / RL ≈ VIN / RL, so doubling VIN doubles the frequency.

Design target for circuit standalone-vfc: 0.05 % linearity over 10 Hz to 4 kHz from 25 mV to 12.5 V input on a 15.0 V supply. CIN from pin 7 to ground filters the input: 0.1 µF suits this case, 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF is enough for most, and 1 µF gives heavier filtering. With matched RC time constants on pins 6 and 7, a step at VIN gives a step in fOUT; with CIN much smaller than CL, a step may halt fOUT for a moment. RIN is 100 kΩ to equal RL, which cancels the comparator bias current and keeps frequency offset small. Resistors should be stable low-tempco types such as metal film; low dielectric absorption matters in the capacitor, and NPO ceramic, polystyrene, Teflon or polypropylene suit it. RS is a 12 kΩ fixed resistor plus a 5 kΩ rheostat, preferably cermet, which trims out the gain tolerance of the converter and of Rt, RL and Ct. The 47 Ω in series with CL adds hysteresis that helps the comparator reach its linearity.

An op amp with feedback capacitor CF does the integration. Its output crossing the threshold on pin 6 starts each timing cycle, and the average current i × 1.1 RtCt × f into the summing node balances −VIN / RIN. The converter's own comparator offset, bias current and offset current then have no effect on offset or accuracy; only the op amp's offset voltage and offset current limit how small a signal can be converted, which makes this the circuit for best small-signal accuracy. The output responds at once to an input change, so fOUT follows VIN as fast as two output pulses can be timed. Pin 1 stays at ground potential whatever VIN or fOUT, so linearity is excellent; in the stand-alone circuit the output impedance of pin 1, which lets i change with VIN, is a main source of non-linearity. Circuit precision-vfc-100k is the same idea adapted for high-speed use.

A C-R network differentiates the input pulses, and each falling edge on pin 6 triggers the timer; pin 1 then delivers an average current of i × 1.1 RtCt × f. In circuit simple-fvc that current is filtered by RL = 100 kΩ and 1 µF: ripple under 10 mV peak, but a 0.1 s time constant and 0.7 s to settle to 0.1 %. In circuit precision-fvc an op amp buffers the output and forms a 2-pole filter: ripple under 5 mV peak above 1 kHz and much faster response, but more ripple than the simple circuit below 200 Hz. The filter time constants are a trade between response and ripple; F-to-V response is inherently slower than V-to-F response.

Long-term integrator: the converter's output feeds a ÷2^N prescaler (CD4020, CD4040 or similar) and then a binary counter (MM74C926 or similar), whose outputs go to a display or computer; a reset line clears both. Basic A-to-D converter: fOUT drives a counter whose count is latched to the outputs; a stable clock of 1.0 Hz to 100 Hz enables the latch and, through a delay, resets the counter. A-to-D with a microprocessor: an LM331A converter's fOUT, optionally through a photoisolator, drives counter A while counter B counts the microprocessor clock, both read over the data bus.

Several isolation schemes are shown for the converter output: a 4N28 or similar optoisolator, its LED fed from +VS through 1 kΩ by fOUT, driving a 2N2222 with a 3.3 kΩ pull-up to +VLOGIC and an inverter, toward a computer, a counter or an LM131 F-to-V converter; a high-voltage pulse transformer into a comparator with hysteresis; a telemetry transmitter and receiver over an RF link; and an LED driven through 1 kΩ into a fiber-optic light pipe, received by a phototransistor and 2N2222 with 3.3 kΩ.
Supply range is 4 V to 40 V. The VS pin needs a 1 µF bypass capacitor of low ESR to ground; X7R is acceptable. At higher supply voltages the bypass capacitor's voltage rating must be high enough.

Put the bypass capacitor as close to the supply pin as possible; on this through-hole package it may sit on the bottom layer. An input filter capacitor to ground also goes close to the supply pin. A ground plane is recommended so that ground stays low in impedance everywhere.
Built-in ESD protection is limited. Store the parts with their leads shorted together or in conductive foam.
